title: Determine the physical and physiological quality of seed

lessons.title: Routine seed testing in a working laboratory
lessons.html:
Workplace scope

This is a substantial workplace module. Over an extended placement in a seed testing laboratory you perform physical and physiological tests on many samples and species, building speed without losing accuracy. Your mentor gradually increases your responsibility until you can run tests independently and have your results accepted for reporting.

Tests you will perform

PhysicalPhysiological
Purity analysisGermination
Other seed determination by numberTetrazolium viability
Moisture content (oven method and meters)Vigour tests such as accelerated ageing, conductivity, cold test
Thousand-seed weightDormancy-breaking treatments where prescribed

Range of species

Aim to cover cereals (maize, wheat, sorghum), oilseeds and legumes (sunflower, soybeans, beans, canola), pasture species (grasses, lucerne) and some vegetables. Each has its own Pure Seed Definition, working sample mass, germination conditions and seedling evaluation features. Keep species notes in your own file.

A typical workflow

  1. Receive and register samples; check labels and seals.
  2. Obtain working samples with approved dividers.
  3. Perform purity, then plant pure seed for germination.
  4. Run moisture promptly from moisture-proof containers.
  5. Make germination first and final counts on the specified days.
  6. Evaluate seedlings and check replicate tolerances.
  7. Calculate results, record raw data, submit for technical review.

Managing workload

Peak periods follow harvest and processing. Plan germination start dates so counts do not all fall on the same day, keep germinators within capacity, and prioritise urgent samples without skipping steps.

Safety

Handle treated seed with gloves and dust control, use guards on grinders, protect against oven heat, handle tetrazolium and other chemicals as their safety data sheets instruct, and keep food out of the laboratory.

lessons.title: Accuracy, problem solving and evidence
lessons.html:
Building reliable results

Your results are checked in several ways: replicate tolerances, repeat tests by colleagues, control samples and ISTA proficiency tests. Use every check as feedback.

Common difficulties and responses

DifficultyResponse
Replicates out of tolerance in germinationCheck substrate moisture, germinator temperature and evaluation; retest as the rules require
Many fresh ungerminated seedsSuspect dormancy; apply prescribed treatment or TZ on remaining seeds
Many abnormal seedlings with cracked seed coatsSuggest mechanical damage; note for the client
Fungal growth spreading in germination testsCheck whether seed-borne or contamination; consider sand or other media where permitted
Purity components do not sum to original mass within limitsRepeat the analysis
Moisture duplicates disagreeCheck sample handling, weighing and oven; repeat

Seedling evaluation skill

Correct classification of normal and abnormal seedlings is the most judgement-heavy part of germination testing. Use the ISTA seedling evaluation handbook, compare with colleagues, and ask your mentor to check borderline seedlings until you are consistently accurate.

Records

Record raw data at the time, with your initials, dates and equipment identification. Correct errors by striking through, never erasing. Your records must allow another analyst to see exactly what you did.

Evidence for assessment

  • Test worksheets you completed across a range of species and tests.
  • Results of repeat tests and control samples compared with yours.
  • Proficiency test participation, where available.
  • Mentor observation checklists and authorisation records.
  • Notes on problems solved and lessons learned.

Evidence must be your own work, current and sufficient across the range.

Key points

  • Cover physical and physiological tests across many species.
  • Follow species-specific rules for working samples and germination conditions.
  • Use tolerance checks, repeats and control samples as feedback.
  • Investigate unusual results such as dormancy or mechanical damage.
  • Record raw data clearly so others can follow your work.
